questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An alga has phycoerythrin, stores floridean starch and lacks motile reproductive cells. Which class is supported by all three observations?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Rhodophyceae.
Why: Red algae commonly possess phycoerythrin and store floridean starch. The lack of flagellated reproductive stages supplies a third consistent clue, so classification does not rest on visible colour alone. These three independent traits are more diagnostic than apparent colour alone, which can vary with lighting or accessory pigments. Their combination also excludes a land-plant life cycle.
Why not the others: (A) Green algae characteristically store starch and chlorophyll predominates. (B) Brown algae have fucoxanthin and laminarin/mannitol reserves. (D) Bryophytes are embryophyte land plants, not this algal class.
Key point: Combine pigments, storage material and life-cycle characters.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.question: In a young root, radial xylem and phloem lie inside a cell layer whose radial walls contain a suberin-rich Casparian strip. What does that layer chiefly regulate?
options: A) Apoplastic entry into the stele by forcing selective membrane crossing
B) Photosynthetic gas exchange in mesophyll
C) Longitudinal phloem pressure from leaf to sink
D) Direct pollen transfer to a stigma
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Endodermal selective entry.
Why: Water moving through cell walls encounters the waterproof strip at the endodermis. To pass inward toward the stele, it must cross a living membrane, where transport can be regulated. The radial vascular arrangement and wall band identify the location. The strip blocks the apoplastic wall route at a continuous endodermal boundary. Water and solutes must enter a symplast through selective membranes before reaching the vascular stele.
Why not the others: (B) Mesophyll is in leaves. (C) Phloem transport occurs after vascular entry and is not the strip's role. (D) Is reproductive transport unrelated to roots.
Key point: Relate wall modification to the path water must take.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A carrier imports Na⁺ and glucose together even when cellular glucose is higher than outside. Blocking the ATP-driven Na⁺ pump eventually stops glucose entry, although the carrier remains present. What powers uptake?
options: B) Direct ATP hydrolysis at the glucose carrier is established by the result
C) Simple diffusion through membrane lipid
D) The Na⁺ gradient maintained by the pump drives coupled glucose transport
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Coupling to the Na⁺ gradient.
Why: Glucose travels uphill, so passive diffusion cannot explain it. The pump uses ATP to maintain a downhill Na⁺ gradient; cotransport can harness that gradient. Blocking the pump removes the stored gradient over time even while the cotransporter protein remains. The Na⁺ gradient provides free energy for cotransport, while ATP is consumed indirectly by the pump that maintains that gradient. Blocking the pump eventually collapses the driver even if the carrier itself still exists.
Why not the others: (A) Glucose is stipulated uphill. (B) The data do not show ATP acting directly on this carrier. (C) Lipid diffusion neither couples Na⁺ nor sustains uphill glucose movement.
Key point: Distinguish direct ATP use from gradient-mediated secondary transport.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Plant growth regulators: identifying gibberellin and auxin from their effects
questions.question: Two separate treatments are tried on plants. (i) A genetically dwarf pea plant sprayed with substance X grows to the height of a normal plant. (ii) Removing the shoot tip of another plant lets its lateral buds grow out, but when substance Y is applied to the cut stump the lateral buds stay suppressed. Which identification of X and Y fits both results?
options: A) X is an auxin; Y is a gibberellin
B) X is a gibberellin; Y is an auxin
C) X is a cytokinin; Y is abscisic acid
D) X is ethylene; Y is a gibberellin
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) X is a gibberellin; Y is an auxin.
Why: Gibberellins promote stem elongation, and many dwarf pea varieties are dwarf because they make too little active gibberellin; supplying it restores normal height. The growing shoot tip makes auxin, which moves down the stem and holds back the lateral buds (apical dominance). Cutting off the tip removes that supply and the buds grow; putting auxin on the stump replaces it and the buds stay suppressed. Each result is a classic test for one hormone, so the two treatments together fix both identities.
Why not the others: (A) swaps the two roles: auxin does not make a genetic dwarf reach normal height, and gibberellin on the stump does not replace the tip's inhibition of lateral buds. (C) Cytokinin promotes cell division and the growth of lateral buds, so it would not be the tip's inhibiting signal, and abscisic acid is a growth inhibitor, not the substance that restores height. (D) Ethylene promotes ripening and senescence and does not restore height in a dwarf; gibberellin is not the apical-dominance signal.
Key point: Gibberellin reverses genetic dwarfism; auxin from the tip causes apical dominance.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Regulation of respiration by CO₂ and H⁺
questions.question: A resting person breathes air enriched with CO₂ for a short time, and the rate and depth of breathing rise. Which sensing mechanism best explains this response?
options: A) Stretch of the diaphragm muscle is the only signal that sets the breathing rhythm
B) A fall in blood oxygen detected by the respiratory rhythm centre is the main signal
C) A chemosensitive area near the rhythm centre in the medulla responds to the rise in CO₂ and H⁺ and signals the rhythm centre
D) Haemoglobin in red cells signals the lungs directly when it carries less oxygen
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A chemosensitive area near the rhythm centre in the medulla responds to the rise in CO₂ and H⁺ and signals the rhythm centre.
Why: Breathing is set by the respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla. Next to it lies a chemosensitive area that is highly sensitive to CO₂ and hydrogen ions. Extra CO₂ in the blood forms carbonic acid and raises H⁺; this area is activated and signals the rhythm centre to make breathing faster and deeper, which removes the extra CO₂. Receptors in the aortic arch and carotid artery also sense CO₂ and H⁺ and send signals to the rhythm centre.
Why not the others: (A) The rhythm comes from the medullary centre, not from stretch of the diaphragm, and stretch does not sense blood gases. (B) Oxygen plays a quite insignificant part in the normal regulation of breathing rhythm; here the oxygen level has not even fallen. (D) Haemoglobin carries gases but is not a sensor and sends no signals.
Key point: Breathing responds mainly to CO₂ and H⁺, not to oxygen.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Bagged flowers of P set no seed after hand self-pollination, but set seed after compatible cross-pollination. P's pollen works on another compatible plant. What inference is supported by these controls?
options: A) Failure is specific to the self combination, consistent with self-incompatibility
B) All P pollen is universally nonviable
C) P ovules never develop following fertilisation
D) Bagging always prevents seed formation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Self-combination rejection.
Why: Cross pollen produces seed on P, establishing that its ovules and bagging procedure can support reproduction. P pollen succeeds elsewhere, establishing viability. The remaining contrast is the self combination, consistent with a self-incompatibility response. The cross-pollination control shows the stigma, ovules and bagging method can produce seeds. Failure only with self pollen supports a self-recognition barrier rather than sterility or accidental damage.
Why not the others: (B) Contradicts successful P pollen use. (C) Contradicts cross seed set. (D) Bagged hand crossing worked.
Key point: Reciprocal controls isolate partner specificity from general infertility.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Transcription direction and antiparallel DNA strands
questions.question: The figure shows a short DNA duplex and a promoter arrow pointing right to left. Assume transcription starts at the rightmost shown base, uses the strand read 3′→5′, and ends after the shown sequence. Which mRNA is made, written 5′→3′?
questions.image_alt: Top strand is 5′-TTA CGA CAT-3′ from left to right; bottom strand is 3′-AAT GCT GTA-5′. A promoter arrow at the right points leftward.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 5′-AUG UCG UAA-3′.
Why: Moving right to left, polymerase must read a 3′→5′ template, which is the top strand in this orientation. Reverse its base order to TAC AGC ATT, then make the complementary RNA AUG UCG UAA. Equivalently, read the bottom coding strand right to left and replace T by U. Both direction and complementarity matter. The top strand is read in its 3′→5′ direction only when moving from right to left. Complementary RNA is synthesized 5′→3′; reverse the written order before replacing template bases with RNA complements.
Why not the others: (A) Copies the displayed top strand in the wrong direction. (B) Copies the bottom strand left to right. (C) reverses without making the RNA complement.
Key point: Select template by promoter direction before transcribing antiparallel bases.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A person loses many helper T lymphocytes while neutrophil numbers initially remain normal. Which impairment best follows from the helper-cell role?
options: A) Only clot formation is lost
B) Coordination of both antibody and cell-mediated adaptive responses weakens
C) All pathogens immediately stop dividing
D) Innate neutrophils become the sole source of antigen-specific antibodies
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Broad adaptive coordination weakens.
Why: Helper T cells signal to other immune cells, including B cells and cytotoxic T cells. Their sustained loss can thus impair both antibody production and cell-mediated responses even when a neutrophil count is initially normal. A count of one innate cell type does not replace adaptive coordination. Helper T-cell signals coordinate antibody production and cellular immunity. Normal neutrophil count does not restore antigen-specific B-cell help, so broad adaptive responses become weaker.
Why not the others: (A) Clotting is not the central helper-cell function. (C) No immune loss sterilises every pathogen. (D) Neutrophils do not secrete antigen-specific antibody.
Key point: Trace effects through the cells a helper population coordinates.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: PCR tubes X and Y have the same template, polymerase, nucleotides and cycling. X has both primers flanking a target; Y lacks the reverse primer. What follows for the defined double-stranded target after many ideal cycles?
options: A) Y must amplify the bounded target more rapidly
B) Both amplify exponentially at the same rate
C) X can amplify it exponentially; Y cannot sustain that bounded two-primer process
D) Neither can extend any DNA strand
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Exponential amplification requires both primers.
Why: Opposed primers define both ends and allow newly synthesized target strands to serve as templates on subsequent cycles. With one missing primer, extension from the remaining primer may occur, but the same bounded double-stranded product cannot repeatedly generate itself by two-primer cycling. Each primer binds an opposite template strand with a 3′ end directed into the target interval. One missing primer permits only linear copying of one side, whereas two define products that amplify exponentially.
Why not the others: (A) Missing a primer does not improve target amplification. (B) Overlooks the second defined end. (D) One primer can still support some extension.
Key point: Distinguish any extension from exponential amplification of a defined amplicon.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Energy partition into detritus, including egested material
questions.question: A plant community has a net primary production of 1000 units in an interval. Herbivores eat 250 units and egest 40% of what they eat as faeces. 100 units remain as standing plant biomass. All the remaining uneaten plant production dies, and both it and the faeces enter the detritus pool. How many units enter detritus?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 750 units.
Given: Net primary production 1000 units; eaten by herbivores 250; egested fraction 40%; standing plant biomass 100.
Formula/Principle: Every unit of net production is eaten, left standing, or dies uneaten. Detritus receives the dead uneaten plant matter plus the faeces.
Step 1: Dead uneaten plant matter = 1000 − 250 − 100 = 650 units.
Step 2: Faeces = 40% of 250 = 100 units.
Step 3: Detritus input = 650 + 100 = 750 units.
Why: Detritus has two sources here. Most comes straight from plants that are never eaten. But food that is eaten is not all assimilated: the egested part passes out as faeces and joins the detritus pool as well. Only the assimilated 150 units stay in the grazing food chain.
Why not the others: (B) 650 counts only the dead plant matter and leaves out the 100 units of faeces. (C) 900 subtracts only the standing biomass from 1000 and treats everything else as detritus, including what the herbivores assimilate. (D) 350 is the sum of what was eaten and what was left standing (250 + 100), which is the part that does not go directly to detritus.
Key point: Detritus = uneaten dead production + egested material.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Pigment needs two independent functional enzymes encoded by A and B; aa or bb blocks the pathway. Two AaBb plants cross. What fraction of offspring is pigmented under complete dominance?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 9/16.
Given: Pigment needs at least one A and at least one B; cross AaBb × AaBb; independent assortment.
Formula/Principle: For independent genes, multiply the probabilities for each gene.
Step 1: Aa × Aa gives A_ with probability 3/4.
Step 2: Bb × Bb gives B_ with probability 3/4.
Step 3: P(pigmented) = P(A_ and B_) = 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16.
Why: Each enzyme works in the same pathway, so losing either one (aa or bb) stops pigment formation. A plant is coloured only if it has a working copy of both genes. This is complementary gene action, and it changes the usual 9:3:3:1 ratio to 9 pigmented : 7 unpigmented.
Why not the others: (A) 3/4 checks only one of the two genes. (B) 1/4 is the chance of being recessive at one gene, not the chance of being dominant at both. (C) 7/16 is the unpigmented fraction, 1 − 9/16.
Key point: Complementary genes give a 9 : 7 ratio.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In strain P, a functional repressor cannot bind its mutated operator; promoter and structural genes work. Strain Q has a normal operator and repressor. With no glucose, compare enzyme expression without and with lactose.
options: A) Both express only without lactose
B) P expresses in both; Q is low without lactose and induced with it
C) P is always off; Q is always on
D) Both remain off because a promoter is present
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) P constitutive, Q inducible.
Why: In P the repressor cannot occupy its DNA site even without inducer, so transcription is not blocked by this control. In Q, bound repressor suppresses transcription until lactose-derived inducer reduces its binding. With glucose absent, the comparison isolates the operator–repressor response rather than catabolite effects. The operator is a cis-acting DNA site, whereas the repressor protein acts in trans. An operator mutation can make a functional repressor unable to block that operon's structural-gene transcription.
Why not the others: (A) Reverses induction. (C) Reverses both strain behaviours. (D) A working promoter permits transcription rather than forbidding it.
Key point: Separate a defective DNA binding site from a defective protein.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Presynaptic stimulation releases normal transmitter in two preparations. A postsynaptic response occurs in P but not Q; direct electrical stimulation of Q's postsynaptic membrane still gives a normal action potential. Where is the likely defect?
options: B) Axonal action-potential generation in Q's postsynaptic membrane
C) Postsynaptic transmitter reception or coupling
D) Complete absence of the presynaptic neuron
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Postsynaptic reception or coupling.
Why: Normal measured release argues against presynaptic failure. Direct electrical stimulation shows that the postsynaptic membrane can still generate an action potential. The missing response lies between arrival of transmitter and electrical activation, such as receptor binding or its coupling to channels. The presynaptic transmitter measurement rules out a failure of release. A response to direct stimulation confirms downstream excitability, narrowing the lesion to transmitter recognition or the postsynaptic receptor process.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) contradict normal transmitter release. (B) contradicts successful direct electrical activation.
Key point: Use a bypass experiment to localise a failure in a signalling chain.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Replication before the two meiotic divisions
questions.question: In ordinary meiosis, when does chromosome DNA replication occur relative to meiosis I and II?
options: A) Once before meiosis I, without replication between the divisions
D) Never, because chromosomes are already visible
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Replication precedes meiosis I only.
Why: S phase copies each chromosome into sister chromatids before homologues separate in the first division. Meiosis II separates those sisters without a second intervening DNA-replication round, allowing haploid products. DNA synthesis occurs once during the preceding interphase. Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes, and meiosis II separates sister chromatids without another intervening S phase.
Why not the others: (B) Would duplicate DNA again between divisions. (C) Comes too late for segregation. (D) Visible chromosomes have already been replicated.
Key point: Distinguish one replication from two consecutive divisions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The figure shows one inherited marker in mother M, child C and candidates P and Q. Assume one allele from each biological parent, precise band sizing and no mutation. What follows from this marker alone?
options: A) Q is established as father with certainty
B) P is compatible and Q excluded, but P is not uniquely proved by one marker
C) Both are excluded because C shares a band with M
D) Each candidate is certainly a parent because each has two bands
questions.image_alt: Gel lanes show M bands 120 and 150, child C 120 and 180, candidate P 160 and 180, and Q 120 and 160, with labelled band-size ladder.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) P compatible, Q excluded.
Why: The child can inherit 120 from M; the 180 allele must then come from the other biological parent. P has 180 and Q does not, so Q is excluded under the assumptions. Many untested people might carry 180, so a single marker cannot establish P uniquely. Every child band must be assigned to a parent under the stated single-marker assumptions. The 180 band cannot be supplied by M, so compare that band, rather than overall resemblance, with candidate lanes.
Why not the others: (A) Q lacks 180. (C) Sharing a maternal allele is expected. (D) Two bands alone show neither transmission nor identity.
Key point: A marker may exclude a candidate without proving another uniquely.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Each C–O bond in CO₂ is polar. Under its linear geometry, what is the molecule's net dipole moment?
options: A) Equal to one bond dipole
B) Zero because equal opposite bond dipoles cancel
C) Twice one bond dipole along the same direction
D) Undefined because carbon is central
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Zero.
Why: The two identical bond dipole vectors lie on the same line but point in opposite directions from the central carbon. Vector addition cancels them even though each individual C–O bond remains polar. Molecular polarity depends on geometry as well as bond polarity. Each C–O bond contributes an equal dipole in an opposite direction along the O=C=O axis. Vector addition gives \(\boldsymbol\mu_{\rm net}=\boldsymbol\mu_1+\boldsymbol\mu_2=0\), even though individual bonds are polar.
Why not the others: (A) Keeps only one bond. (C) Adds magnitudes without directions. (D) A central atom does not prevent vector addition.
Key point: Sum bond dipoles as vectors.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The figure shows small octahedral splitting for complex X and large splitting for Y, both d⁶ at the same metal oxidation state. Under the simple crystal-field model, how many unpaired electrons do X and Y have?
questions.image_alt: Two octahedral energy diagrams have three lower t2g and two upper eg levels; X has gap Δsmall less than pairing energy, Y gap Δlarge greater than pairing energy. No electrons are drawn.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Four and zero.
Why: The small splitting in X makes occupation of the upper eg levels preferable to pairing too early: high-spin d⁶ is t₂g⁴e_g², with four unpaired electrons. The large gap in Y favours pairing in t₂g first: t₂g⁶e_g⁰ has no unpaired electrons. The figure supplies the energetic comparison but leaves the filling to be reasoned out. For d⁶, the high-spin small-gap arrangement leaves more electrons unpaired in both lower and upper sets; the large-gap case pairs in t₂g first. Compare crystal-field energy cost with pairing energy, not merely total d-electron count.
Why not the others: (A) Reverses complexes. (B) Counts only eg electrons in X and invents unpaired electrons in Y. (C) Treats all six d electrons as independently unpaired despite only five orbitals.
Key point: Compare Δ with pairing energy before filling orbitals.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Half-filled d subshell in common ions
questions.question: Between Mn²⁺ (Z=25) and Fe²⁺ (Z=26), which has a half-filled 3d subshell and how many 3d electrons does it contain?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Mn²⁺, 3d⁵.
Why: Neutral Mn is [Ar]3d⁵4s² and neutral Fe is [Ar]3d⁶4s². Forming 2+ ions removes the two 4s electrons first, leaving Mn²⁺ 3d⁵ and Fe²⁺ 3d⁶. Five d electrons give a half-filled five-orbital subshell. The 4s electrons are removed before 3d electrons for these cations. Thus Mn²⁺ remains 3d⁵ while Fe²⁺ becomes 3d⁶; only the former has the half-filled d subshell.
Why not the others: (B) Assigns Mn's count to Fe. (C) Retains 4s electrons as 3d. (D) Correctly counts Fe but six is not half-filled.
Key point: Remove ns electrons before (n−1)d in these cations.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Why is first ionisation energy of N higher than O, despite O's larger nuclear charge?
options: A) Nitrogen has a complete 2p⁶ subshell
C) Oxygen has a paired 2p orbital with extra repulsion relative to N's 2p³ arrangement
D) Nitrogen's outer electrons occupy n=3
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Pairing repulsion in O.
Why: N has one electron in each of the three 2p orbitals, a relatively stable half-filled arrangement. O adds a fourth 2p electron that pairs in one orbital; repulsion makes removal of one electron easier than a simple nuclear-charge trend suggests. Oxygen's fourth 2p electron shares one orbital and experiences extra electron–electron repulsion. Removing it relieves a pairing cost, whereas removing from nitrogen disrupts a stable singly occupied pattern.
Why not the others: (A) N is 2p³, not 2p⁶. (B) O is 2p⁴. (D) Both valence shells are n=2.
Key point: Consider orbital occupancy when a periodic trend has an exception.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A proton of mass m, charge e and alpha particle of mass 4m, charge 2e start from rest and traverse the same accelerating potential V nonrelativistically. Find λproton/λα.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) √8.
Given: Proton: mass \(m\), charge \(e\). Alpha particle: mass \(4m\), charge \(2e\). Both start from rest and cross the same potential difference \(V\).
Formula/Principle: Kinetic energy gained \(=qV\); \(p=\sqrt{2m_{\text{particle}}\,qV}\); \(\lambda=h/p\).
Step 1: \(p_p=\sqrt{2\,m\,eV}\).
Step 2: \(p_\alpha=\sqrt{2\,(4m)(2e)V}=\sqrt{16\,m\,eV}\).
Step 3: \(\lambda_p/\lambda_\alpha=p_\alpha/p_p\).
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_\alpha}=\frac{p_\alpha}{p_p}=\sqrt{\frac{2(4m)(2e)V}{2\,m\,e\,V}}=\sqrt8=2\sqrt2\]
Why: Both the mass and the charge differ. The charge sets how much kinetic energy each particle gains from the same voltage, and the mass then sets the momentum for that energy. The alpha particle ends up with \(\sqrt8\) times the proton's momentum, so its wavelength is shorter by the same factor.
Why not the others: (A) 2 is \(\sqrt4\): it uses only the mass ratio and ignores the charge. (C) \(\sqrt2\) uses only the charge ratio and ignores the mass. (D) 8 is the ratio of \(p^2\), with the square root left out.
Key point: \(\lambda=h/\sqrt{2mqV}\), so \(\lambda\propto1/\sqrt{mq}\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A+B→C uses 0.10 mol A and 0.16 mol B in a 1:1 reaction, isolating C at 80% theoretical yield. Then 2C→D isolates D at 75% of the theoretical yield from the isolated C. How many moles D result?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.030 mol.
Given: 0.10 mol A and 0.16 mol B; \(\ce{A + B -> C}\) at 80% yield; \(\ce{2C -> D}\) at 75% yield.
Formula/Principle: Find the limiting reagent, apply the mole ratio, then apply each percentage yield in turn.
Step 1: A is limiting (0.10 < 0.16), so theoretical C \(=0.10\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Step 2: Isolated C \(=0.80\times0.10=0.080\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Step 3: Theoretical D \(=0.080/2=0.040\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Step 4: Isolated D \(=0.75\times0.040=0.030\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Worked derivation: \[n_D=0.75\times\frac{0.80\times0.10}{2}=0.75\times0.040=0.030\ \mathrm{mol}\]
Why: The excess B plays no part once A is used up. The second reaction starts from the C actually isolated, not the theoretical amount, and it needs two C for each D. So both yields and the 2 : 1 ratio must all be applied.
Why not the others: (A) 0.060 leaves out the 2 : 1 ratio of the second step (0.080 × 0.75). (B) 0.040 leaves out the 75% yield of the second step. (C) 0.075 applies only the 75% yield to 0.10 mol and leaves out both the first yield and the 2 : 1 ratio.
Key point: Overall amount = limiting moles × each mole ratio × each fractional yield.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: At the para position, compare nitro- and methoxy-substituted benzoic acids with benzoic acid under the same conditions. Which is expected to be strongest?
options: A) p-Nitrobenzoic acid, because the electron-withdrawing group stabilises benzoate
B) p-Methoxybenzoic acid, because resonance donation stabilises benzoate
C) Benzoic acid, because substitution can never affect acidity
D) All exactly equal, because each has a COOH group
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) p-Nitrobenzoic acid.
Why: Nitro withdraws electron density through inductive and resonance effects and helps stabilise the negatively charged conjugate base. At para, methoxy resonance donation tends to oppose this stabilisation. Acid strength follows how favourably deprotonation products are stabilised under comparable conditions. A para nitro group withdraws through both induction and resonance, stabilising the carboxylate relative to neutral acid. A methoxy group donates by resonance at para, tending to destabilise that conjugate base in the relevant comparison.
Why not the others: (B) Donation does not stabilise the anion in the claimed way. (C) Ring substituents transmit electronic effects. (D) The same acidic group can have different environments.
Key point: Compare conjugate-base stabilisation, with substituent position specified.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The figure shows the two distinct carbonyl products from reductive ozonolysis of one acyclic alkene molecule, one molecule of each. Which alkene reconstructs the original carbon skeleton?
questions.image_alt: Two labelled product structures are methanal H–C(=O)–H and ethanal CH3–C(=O)–H; one of each forms per alkene.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Propene.
Why: Each carbonyl carbon was originally one carbon of the C=C bond. Rejoining the methanal carbon and ethanal carbon by a double bond, replacing their carbonyl oxygens, gives CH₂=CH–CH₃. The fragments account for all three carbons in propene. Reductive ozonolysis splits the C=C and puts one oxygen at each original alkene carbon. Reconnecting the two carbonyl carbons and removing the oxygens reconstructs the original carbon skeleton and substituent placement.
Why not the others: (A) Gives two methanals. (B) Gives two ethanals. (D) Gives methanal plus propanone rather than ethanal.
Key point: Reconstruct the two former alkene carbons from their separate carbonyl products.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Under mild conditions that permit ordinary SN2 substitution of a primary bromoalkane by hydroxide, bromobenzene is much less reactive. Which structural distinction matters most?
options: A) Bromobenzene has no C–Br bond
B) Resonance gives aryl C–Br partial double-bond character and sp² carbon disfavors backside SN2 attack
C) A primary bromoalkane has a benzene ring
D) Bromobenzene is freely ionised into phenyl cations in water
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Aryl C–Br is resistant to ordinary SN2.
Why: Conjugation with the ring gives the C–Br bond partial double-bond character, and backside approach to an sp² aryl carbon is geometrically unfavourable. These features distinguish aryl from primary alkyl halides under the stipulated mild conditions. Ordinary SN2 requires attack at a tetrahedral carbon from behind the leaving group. Chlorobenzene binds Cl to sp² aryl carbon and has resonance-strengthened C–Cl character, so that mechanism is inaccessible under the mild comparison.
Why not the others: (A) The bond exists. (C) Primary bromoalkane is not aromatic. (D) Stable free phenyl cations do not form readily in water.
Key point: Do not transfer an alkyl-halide mechanism uncritically to an aryl halide.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Phenol forms a salt with ordinary aqueous NaOH, whereas ethanol is not comparably deprotonated. What explains the difference?
options: A) Ethanol contains no O–H bond
C) Hydroxide reacts only with aromatic C–C bonds
D) Phenoxide is resonance-stabilised relative to an alkoxide
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Phenoxide stabilisation.
Why: Deprotonating phenol gives an anion whose charge can delocalise into the aromatic system. Ethoxide lacks that resonance stabilisation, so ethanol is a substantially weaker acid under the usual qualitative comparison. Phenoxide has additional resonance contributors that spread its negative charge into the aromatic ring. Ethoxide is confined largely to oxygen, making its formation by aqueous hydroxide far less favourable.
Why not the others: (A) Ethanol has an O–H group. (B) Phenol is not an aldehyde. (C) The relevant reaction is proton transfer at oxygen.
Key point: Compare conjugate bases to explain an acidity contrast.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Charge of hydrolysed amino acids above pI
questions.question: Complete hydrolysis of Gly–Ala yields free glycine and alanine. At pH well above both isoelectric points, what net-charge tendency does each free amino acid have?
options: C) Glycine positive, alanine negative solely due to side chains
D) Both must be net neutral at every pH
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both tend net negative.
Why: Above each isoelectric point, deprotonation shifts the balance toward anionic forms. Glycine and alanine side chains do not introduce opposite ordinary ionisation behaviour, and hydrolysis frees their amino and carboxyl groups from the peptide bond. At high pH the carboxyl groups are deprotonated and the ammonium groups tend to lose protons. Evaluate each free amino acid's charge rather than assuming the intact peptide retains the same termini.
Why not the others: (B) Positive net charge is favoured at lower pH. (C) The non-ionising side chains do not reverse signs. (D) Net charge changes with pH.
Key point: Evaluate the free products at the stated pH, not the intact peptide.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: AgCl has Ksp=1.0×10⁻¹⁰ at the stated temperature. By what factor is its molar solubility in 0.10 M NaCl smaller than its molar solubility in pure water? Neglect the change in [Cl⁻] caused by the dissolving AgCl in the NaCl solution.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 10⁴.
Given: \(K_{sp}(\ce{AgCl})=1.0\times10^{-10}\); \([\ce{Cl-}]=0.10\ \mathrm M\) from NaCl.
Formula/Principle: \(K_{sp}=[\ce{Ag+}][\ce{Cl-}]\); the solubility equals \([\ce{Ag+}]\) at equilibrium.
Step 1: Pure water: \(s_0^2=10^{-10}\), so \(s_0=1.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm M\).
Step 2: In 0.10 M NaCl: \(s=K_{sp}/[\ce{Cl-}]=10^{-10}/0.10=1.0\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm M\).
Step 3: Ratio \(=s_0/s\).
Worked derivation: \[\frac{s_0}{s}=\frac{1.0\times10^{-5}}{1.0\times10^{-9}}=10^{4}\]
Why: Chloride from the NaCl is a common ion. By Le Chatelier's principle it pushes the dissolving equilibrium back towards solid AgCl, so much less silver chloride dissolves. The approximation is safe because the \(10^{-9}\ \mathrm M\) of chloride added by the dissolving salt is negligible next to 0.10 M.
Why not the others: (A) \(10^2\) has no basis in these numbers; it would need a solubility of \(10^{-7}\ \mathrm M\) in the NaCl solution. (B) \(10^5\) compares \(s_0=10^{-5}\) with \(K_{sp}=10^{-10}\), forgetting to divide by the chloride concentration. (D) \(10^9\) is \(1/s\), not a ratio of the two solubilities.
Key point: With a common ion at concentration C, \(s\approx K_{sp}/C\).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: At fixed temperature and composition, a liquid mixture's total vapour pressure exceeds its ideal Raoult-law prediction. Which interaction pattern is consistent with this positive deviation?
options: A) Unlike A–B attractions must be stronger than like pairs
B) Unlike A–B attractions are weaker on average, permitting easier escape
C) The mixture has zero vapour pressure
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Weaker unlike interactions.
Why: Mixing replaces some A–A and B–B neighbours with A–B neighbours. When those unlike contacts are less favourable on average, molecules escape more readily than the ideal reference predicts, raising total vapour pressure. Weaker unlike attractions make molecules escape more readily from the liquid than in the ideal mixture. A higher observed total vapour pressure is therefore a positive deviation; it does not imply that every component's mole fraction increased.
Why not the others: (A) Stronger unlike attractions generally cause negative deviation. (C) Contradicts pressure above a positive ideal prediction. (D) Positive deviation need not mean zero attraction.
Key point: Interpret vapour-pressure deviations through unlike contacts.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Copper sulfate electrolysis with inert electrodes
questions.question: Aqueous CuSO₄ is electrolysed with inert Pt electrodes under conditions where Cu²⁺ deposits at the cathode and water is oxidised at the anode. Which primary products follow?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Copper and oxygen.
Why: Cu²⁺ gains electrons at the cathode to form solid Cu. The stipulated anodic water oxidation releases O₂; sulfate remains in solution and does not become a gas. The electrode reactions must be assigned separately. At inert electrodes, the cathode and anode host separate reduction and oxidation half-reactions. Electrons consumed by Cu²⁺ deposition are balanced by electrons released from water oxidation under the specified conditions.
Why not the others: (A) Ignores the specified copper deposition. (B) Sulfate reduction is not the anode reaction. (C) Gaseous sulfate is not an ordinary product.
Key point: Identify reduction and oxidation at their respective electrodes.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: 50.0 mL of 1.00 M strong monoprotic acid and 50.0 mL of 0.500 M strong base react fully in an insulated calorimeter. The final 100 g of solution warms by 3.4 °C; use c=4.20 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and neglect the heat capacity of the calorimeter. Assuming only neutralisation causes the measured heat, find the enthalpy change per mole of water formed.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) −57.1 kJ/mol.
Given: Acid \(=0.0500\ \mathrm L\times1.00\ \mathrm M=0.0500\ \mathrm{mol}\); base \(=0.0500\ \mathrm L\times0.500\ \mathrm M=0.0250\ \mathrm{mol}\); mass 100 g; \(c=4.20\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}K^{-1}}\); \(\Delta T=3.4\ \mathrm K\).
Formula/Principle: \(q_{\text{solution}}=mc\,\Delta T\); \(q_{\text{reaction}}=-q_{\text{solution}}\); divide by the moles of water formed.
Step 1: The base is limiting, so water formed \(=0.0250\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Step 2: \(q_{\text{solution}}=100\times4.20\times3.4=1428\ \mathrm J\).
Step 3: \(q_{\text{reaction}}=-1428\ \mathrm J=-1.428\ \mathrm{kJ}\).
Worked derivation: \[\Delta H=\frac{-1.428\ \mathrm{kJ}}{0.0250\ \mathrm{mol}}=-57.1\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\]
Why: The solution warms, so the reaction gives out heat and its enthalpy change is negative. Only 0.0250 mol of water can form because the base runs out first; the extra acid simply stays in solution. The answer matches the known value for a strong acid with a strong base, about −57 kJ per mole of water.
Why not the others: (B) −28.6 kJ/mol divides the heat by all 0.0500 mol of acid instead of the 0.0250 mol that reacted. (C) +57.1 kJ/mol has the wrong sign; a temperature rise means heat is released. (D) −114.2 kJ/mol halves the reacting amount a second time (dividing by 0.0125 mol).
Key point: Divide the heat by the moles of the limiting reagent, and give an exothermic change a negative sign.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Tangent-line parameter for an off-origin circle
questions.question: The circle x²+y²−6x−8y=0 is touched by a line 3x+4y=k. What are the possible values of k?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0 and 50.
Given: \(x^2+y^2-6x-8y=0,\quad3x+4y=k\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{tangent}\iff d(\text{centre},\text{line})=r\)
Step 1: \((x-3)^2+(y-4)^2=25\Rightarrow\text{centre }(3,4),\ r=5\)
Step 2: \(d=\dfrac{|3(3)+4(4)-k|}{\sqrt{3^2+4^2}}=\dfrac{|25-k|}{5}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{|25-k|}{5}=5\Rightarrow|25-k|=25\)
Worked derivation: \[25-k=\pm25\Rightarrow k=0\ \text{or}\ k=50\]
Check: \[k=0:\ (0,0)\ \text{on circle and on }3x+4y=0;\ \text{radius direction }(3,4)\perp\text{line}\]
Why: \(d<r:\ 2\ \text{points};\quad d=r:\ 1\ \text{point}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(|k|=25\) (centre taken as origin); (B) \(|25-k|=20\ne25\); (C) \(k=25\Rightarrow d=0\ne5\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{|ah+bk'-c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}=r\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: The point (1,1) lies on x²+xy+y²=3. Where does its tangent meet the x-axis?
options: D) It is parallel to the x-axis
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) x=2.
Given: \(x^2+xy+y^2=3,\quad(1,1)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}:\ 2x+y+xy'+2yy'=0\)
Step 1: \(y'=-\dfrac{2x+y}{x+2y}\)
Step 2: \(y'(1,1)=-\dfrac{3}{3}=-1\)
Step 3: \(y-1=-(x-1)\Rightarrow x+y=2\)
Worked derivation: \[y=0\Rightarrow x=2\]
Check: \[1^2+1\cdot1+1^2=3;\qquad(2,0):\ 2+0=2\]
Why: \(\text{tangent slope}=\left.\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right|_{(1,1)}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(x=-2:\ -2+0\ne2\); (B) \(x=1:\ 1+0\ne2\); (D) \(y'=-1\ne0\).
Key point: \(F(x,y)=c\Rightarrow y'=-\dfrac{F_x}{F_y}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Open-box volume optimisation with a feasible domain
questions.question: Equal squares of side x are cut from the four corners of a 12 cm by 8 cm rectangle, and the sides are folded into an open box. Which x gives maximum volume?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (10−2√7)/3 cm.
Given: \(12\ \mathrm{cm}\times8\ \mathrm{cm},\quad\text{corner squares of side }x,\quad0<x<4\)
Formula/Principle: \(V=x(12-2x)(8-2x),\quad V'=0,\ V''<0\)
Step 1: \(V=4x^3-40x^2+96x\)
Step 2: \(V'=12x^2-80x+96=4(3x^2-20x+24)\)
Step 3: \(3x^2-20x+24=0\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{20\pm\sqrt{400-288}}{6}=\dfrac{10\pm2\sqrt7}{3}\)
Step 4: \(\dfrac{10+2\sqrt7}{3}\approx5.10>4;\quad\dfrac{10-2\sqrt7}{3}\approx1.57\in(0,4)\)
Worked derivation: \[V''=24x-80,\quad V''(1.57)\approx-42.3<0\Rightarrow x=\frac{10-2\sqrt7}{3}\ \mathrm{cm}\]
Check: \[V(1.57)\approx1.57\times8.86\times4.86\approx67.6\ \mathrm{cm^3}>V(2)=2\times8\times4=64\ \mathrm{cm^3}\]
Why: \(8-2x>0\Rightarrow x<4;\quad V(0)=V(4)=0\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{10+2\sqrt7}{3}\approx5.10>4\); (C) \(V'(2)=4(12-40+24)=-16\ne0\); (D) \(V(4)=0\).
Key point: \(V'(x)=0\ \text{and}\ x\in\text{feasible interval}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Evaluate ∫₀¹[x/(1+x²)−x/(1+x)]dx.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (3/2)ln2−1.
Given: \(I=\displaystyle\int_0^1\left[\frac{x}{1+x^2}-\frac{x}{1+x}\right]dx\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x}{1+x^2}dx=\tfrac12\ln(1+x^2),\quad\frac{x}{1+x}=1-\frac{1}{1+x}\)
Step 1: \(\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{x}{1+x^2}dx=\left[\tfrac12\ln(1+x^2)\right]_0^1=\tfrac12\ln2\)
Step 2: \(\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{x}{1+x}dx=\left[x-\ln(1+x)\right]_0^1=1-\ln2\)
Worked derivation: \[I=\frac12\ln2-(1-\ln2)=\frac32\ln2-1\]
Check: \[\tfrac32(0.6931)-1=0.0397>0;\qquad\frac{x}{1+x^2}\ge\frac{x}{1+x}\ \text{on }[0,1]\]
Why: \(0\le x\le1\Rightarrow x^2\le x\Rightarrow\dfrac{x}{1+x^2}\ge\dfrac{x}{1+x}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(1-\tfrac32\ln2<0\) (order reversed); (C) \(\tfrac12\ln2\) (second integral omitted); (D) \(\ln2-1=-\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{x}{1+x}dx\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{x}{1+x}=1-\dfrac{1}{1+x}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Domain of a composition with root and denominator
questions.question: Let f(x)=√(x−1) and g(t)=1/(t−2), both real-valued where defined. What is the domain of g∘f?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) x≥1 with x≠5.
Given: \(f(x)=\sqrt{x-1},\quad g(t)=\dfrac{1}{t-2}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\operatorname{dom}(g\circ f)=\{x\in\operatorname{dom}f:\ f(x)\in\operatorname{dom}g\}\)
Step 1: \(\operatorname{dom}f:\ x-1\ge0\Rightarrow x\ge1\)
Step 2: \(f(x)\ne2:\ \sqrt{x-1}\ne2\Rightarrow x\ne5\)
Worked derivation: \[\operatorname{dom}(g\circ f)=[1,5)\cup(5,\infty)\]
Check: \[x=1:\ g(f(1))=\frac{1}{0-2}=-\frac12;\qquad x=5:\ \frac{1}{2-2}\ \text{undefined}\]
Why: \(g(f(x))=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x-1}-2}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(x=1\in\operatorname{dom},\ x=5\notin\operatorname{dom}\); (B) \(x=2:\ \dfrac{1}{1-2}=-1\ \text{defined}\); (C) \(x=0:\ \sqrt{-1}\notin\mathbb R\).
Key point: \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\ \text{and}\ f(x)\in\operatorname{dom}g\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Scalar triple product with prescribed volume
questions.question: Vectors a=(1,1,0), b=(1,0,1), c=(t,1,1) span a parallelepiped of volume 3. What real t-values are possible?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) −1 and 5.
Given: \(\mathbf a=(1,1,0),\quad\mathbf b=(1,0,1),\quad\mathbf c=(t,1,1),\quad V=3\)
Formula/Principle: \(V=|\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c)|\)
Step 1: \(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c=(0\cdot1-1\cdot1,\ 1\cdot t-1\cdot1,\ 1\cdot1-0\cdot t)=(-1,\ t-1,\ 1)\)
Step 2: \(\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c)=-1+(t-1)+0=t-2\)
Step 3: \(|t-2|=3\)
Worked derivation: \[t-2=\pm3\Rightarrow t=5\ \text{or}\ t=-1\]
Check: \[\begin{vmatrix}1&1&0\\1&0&1\\5&1&1\end{vmatrix}=1(0-1)-1(1-5)+0=3\]
Why: \(V=|\det[\mathbf a\ \mathbf b\ \mathbf c]|\)
Why not the others: (A) \(t=2\Rightarrow V=0\); (B) \(|t+2|=3\) (sign of 2 reversed); (D) \(t=1\Rightarrow V=|1-2|=1\ne3\).
Key point: \(|x-p|=q\Rightarrow x=p\pm q\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A has rows R₁,R₂,R₃ and det A=3. Matrix B has rows R₁+R₂, R₂+R₃, R₃+R₁ in that order; then its first and third rows are interchanged. Find det B.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) −6.
Given: \(\det A=3;\quad\text{rows of }B_0:\ R_1+R_2,\ R_2+R_3,\ R_3+R_1;\quad B=B_0\ \text{with rows 1, 3 interchanged}\)
Formula/Principle: \(B_0=TA,\quad\det(TA)=\det T\,\det A,\quad\text{row interchange}\Rightarrow\det\to-\det\)
Step 1: \(T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix}\)
Step 2: \(\det T=1(1\cdot1-1\cdot0)-1(0\cdot1-1\cdot1)+0=1+1=2\)
Step 3: \(\det B_0=2\times3=6\)
Worked derivation: \[\det B=-\det B_0=-6\]
Check: \[A=\operatorname{diag}(3,1,1):\ B_0=\begin{pmatrix}3&1&0\\0&1&1\\3&0&1\end{pmatrix},\ \det B_0=3(1)-1(0-3)=6\]
Why: \(\det\ \text{is linear in each row and alternating}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(+6\) (interchange omitted); (C) \(-3\) (\(\det T=1\)); (D) \(+3\) (\(\det T=1\), interchange omitted).
Key point: \(\det(R_1+R_2,\ R_2+R_3,\ R_3+R_1)=2\det(R_1,R_2,R_3)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Three balls are drawn together from a bag with 4 red and 3 blue balls. Given that at least two drawn balls are red, what is the probability that all three are red?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2/11.
Given: \(4R,\ 3B;\quad3\ \text{drawn together}\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(X|Y)=\dfrac{n(X\cap Y)}{n(Y)}\)
Step 1: \(n(3R)=\dbinom43=4\)
Step 2: \(n(2R,1B)=\dbinom42\dbinom31=6\times3=18\)
Step 3: \(n(\ge2R)=18+4=22\)
Worked derivation: \[P(3R\,|\,\ge2R)=\frac{4}{22}=\frac{2}{11}\]
Check: \[\binom73=35=\underbrace{1}_{0R}+\underbrace{12}_{1R}+\underbrace{18}_{2R}+\underbrace{4}_{3R}\]
Why: \(\{3R\}\subset\{\ge2R\}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\dfrac{4}{35}=P(3R)\) (condition ignored); (C) \(\tfrac12\) (2R and 3R taken as equally likely); (D) \(\dfrac{6}{22}=\dfrac{3}{11}\) (\(\binom42\) for \(\binom43\)).
Key point: \(P(X|Y)=\dfrac{P(X\cap Y)}{P(Y)}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A path from (0,0) to (5,4) uses only unit right or up steps. How many such paths avoid the point (2,2)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 66.
Given: \((0,0)\to(5,4),\quad\text{steps R, U};\quad\text{avoid }(2,2)\)
Formula/Principle: \(N\big((0,0)\to(a,b)\big)=\dbinom{a+b}{a}\)
Step 1: \(N_{\text{all}}=\dbinom94=126\)
Step 2: \(N\big((0,0)\to(2,2)\big)=\dbinom42=6\)
Step 3: \(N\big((2,2)\to(5,4)\big)=\dbinom{3+2}{2}=10\)
Step 4: \(N_{\text{through}}=6\times10=60\)
Worked derivation: \[N=126-60=66\]
Check: \[\binom94=\frac{9\cdot8\cdot7\cdot6}{24}=126\]
Why: \(N_{\text{avoid}}=N_{\text{all}}-N_{\text{through}}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(126=N_{\text{all}}\); (B) \(60=N_{\text{through}}\); (C) \(6\times6=36\) (\(\binom42\) for \(\binom52\)).
Key point: \(N_{\text{through }P}=N(\text{start}\to P)\times N(P\to\text{end})\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Vanishing coefficient followed by adjacent term
questions.question: For integer n≥4, the coefficient of x³ in (1+x)^n(1−x) vanishes. What is the coefficient of x⁴ in the same polynomial?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) −5.
Given: \([x^3]\,(1+x)^n(1-x)=0,\quad n\ge4\)
Formula/Principle: \([x^r]\,(1+x)^n(1-x)=\dbinom nr-\dbinom n{r-1}\)
Step 1: \(\dbinom n3-\dbinom n2=0\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{\binom n3}{\binom n2}=\dfrac{n-2}{3}=1\Rightarrow n=5\)
Worked derivation: \[[x^4]=\binom54-\binom53=5-10=-5\]
Check: \[(1+x)^5(1-x)=1+4x+5x^2+0x^3-5x^4-4x^5-x^6\]
Why: \((1+x)^n(1-x)=(1+x)^n-x(1+x)^n\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dbinom53-\dbinom54=+5\) (order reversed); (B) \(-\dbinom53=-10\) (\(\binom54\) omitted); (D) \([x^3]=0\ne[x^4]\).
Key point: \(\dbinom nr=\dbinom n{r-1}\iff n=2r-1\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: What is Σₖ₌₁⁴ 1/[k(k+2)]?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 17/30.
Given: \(S=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{4}\frac{1}{k(k+2)}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{1}{k(k+2)}=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac1k-\dfrac{1}{k+2}\right)\)
Step 1: \(S=\dfrac12\left[\left(1-\tfrac13\right)+\left(\tfrac12-\tfrac14\right)+\left(\tfrac13-\tfrac15\right)+\left(\tfrac14-\tfrac16\right)\right]\)
Step 2: \(S=\dfrac12\left(1+\tfrac12-\tfrac15-\tfrac16\right)\)
Worked derivation: \[S=\frac12\cdot\frac{30+15-6-5}{30}=\frac12\cdot\frac{34}{30}=\frac{17}{30}\]
Check: \[\frac13+\frac18+\frac1{15}+\frac1{24}=\frac{40+15+8+5}{120}=\frac{68}{120}=\frac{17}{30}\]
Why: \(\dfrac1k-\dfrac{1}{k+2}=\dfrac{2}{k(k+2)}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{11}{24}=\dfrac13+\dfrac18\) (two terms); (C) \(\dfrac{21}{40}=\dfrac13+\dfrac18+\dfrac1{15}\) (three terms); (D) \(\dfrac45=\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{4}\dfrac{1}{k(k+1)}\).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{k(k+2)}=\frac12\left(\frac32-\frac1{n+1}-\frac1{n+2}\right)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For which real k does x²−(k+1)x+(k−2)=0 have one negative root and one positive root strictly greater than 2?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0<k<2.
Given: \(p(x)=x^2-(k+1)x+(k-2),\quad r_1<0,\quad r_2>2\)
Formula/Principle: \(r_1r_2<0;\quad r_1<2<r_2\iff p(2)<0\)
Step 1: \(r_1r_2=k-2<0\Rightarrow k<2\)
Step 2: \(p(2)=4-2(k+1)+(k-2)=-k\)
Step 3: \(p(2)<0\Rightarrow k>0\)
Worked derivation: \[0<k<2\]
Check: \[k=1:\ x^2-2x-1=0,\quad x=1\pm\sqrt2\approx-0.41,\ 2.41\]
Why: \(p(0)=k-2<0\ \text{and}\ p(2)=-k<0\Rightarrow r_1<0<2<r_2\)
Why not the others: (B) \(k=-1:\ x^2-3=0,\ r_2=\sqrt3<2\); (C) \(k=0:\ x^2-x-2=0,\ r_2=2\not>2\); (D) \(k=3:\ r_1r_2=1>0\).
Key point: \(p(\alpha)<0\ \text{and}\ p(\beta)<0\Rightarrow r_1<\alpha<\beta<r_2\ \ (\text{leading coefficient}>0)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Population variance from mean and sum of squares
questions.question: Five observations have arithmetic mean 4 and sum of squares 125. What is their population standard deviation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3.
Given: \(n=5,\quad\bar x=4,\quad\displaystyle\sum x_i^2=125\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sigma^2=\dfrac1n\displaystyle\sum x_i^2-\bar x^2\)
Step 1: \(\sigma^2=\dfrac{125}{5}-4^2=25-16=9\)
Worked derivation: \[\sigma=\sqrt9=3\]
Check: \[\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2=\sum x_i^2-2\bar x\sum x_i+n\bar x^2=125-2(4)(20)+5(16)=45,\qquad\frac{45}{5}=9\]
Why: \(\dfrac1n\displaystyle\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2=\dfrac1n\sum x_i^2-\bar x^2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(9=\sigma^2\); (B) \(45=125-5(16)=\displaystyle\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\); (C) \(\sqrt{45}\) (\(\div n\) omitted).
Key point: \(\sigma=\sqrt{\overline{x^2}-\bar x^{\,2}}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Eliminating constants from a solution family
questions.question: Which differential equation is satisfied by every function y=C₁e^x+C₂e^(−x), for arbitrary constants C₁,C₂?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) y″=y.
Given: \(y=C_1e^{x}+C_2e^{-x}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{two arbitrary constants}\Rightarrow\text{second-order equation}\)
Step 1: \(y'=C_1e^{x}-C_2e^{-x}\)
Step 2: \(y''=C_1e^{x}+C_2e^{-x}\)
Worked derivation: \[y''=y\]
Check: \[C_1=1,\ C_2=0:\ y=e^x,\ y''=e^x=y;\qquad C_1=0,\ C_2=1:\ y=e^{-x},\ y''=e^{-x}=y\]
Why: \(y''-y=0\ \text{for all }C_1,\ C_2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(y'-y=-2C_2e^{-x}\ne0\); (B) \(y''+y=2y\ne0\); (D) \(y'=C_1e^x-C_2e^{-x}\ne0\).
Key point: \(\text{order of the differential equation}=\text{number of arbitrary constants}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Continuous extension and derivative at a point
questions.question: Define f(x)=sin(2x)/x for x≠0 and f(0)=k. For continuity at zero, what are k and f′(0)?
options: D) No value of k works
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) k=2, f′(0)=0.
Given: \(f(x)=\dfrac{\sin2x}{x}\ (x\ne0),\quad f(0)=k\)
Formula/Principle: \(k=\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}f(x),\quad f'(0)=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{f(x)-f(0)}{x}\)
Step 1: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin2x}{x}=2\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin2x}{2x}=2\Rightarrow k=2\)
Step 2: \(f'(0)=\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin2x-2x}{x^2}\)
Step 3: \(\sin2x=2x-\dfrac{(2x)^3}{6}+\dots\Rightarrow\sin2x-2x=-\dfrac43x^3+\dots\)
Worked derivation: \[f'(0)=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{-\tfrac43x^3}{x^2}=\lim_{x\to0}\left(-\frac43x\right)=0\]
Check: \[f(-x)=\frac{\sin(-2x)}{-x}=f(x)\Rightarrow f\ \text{even}\Rightarrow f'(0)=0\]
Why: \(f\ \text{even and differentiable at }0\Rightarrow f'(0)=0\)
Why not the others: (A) \(k=\sin0=0\ne2\); (C) \(f'(0)=2\) (\(k\) repeated); (D) \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}f(x)=2\ \text{exists}\).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin ax}{x}=a\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: From the same height, one ball is released horizontally and another is dropped from rest at the same instant. Neglect air resistance. Which lands first on level ground?
options: D) It depends on horizontal speed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both simultaneously.
Given: \(\text{same height }h;\quad u_y=0\ \text{for both};\quad u_x\ne0\ \text{for ball 1}\)
Formula/Principle: \(y=h-\tfrac12gt^2\ \ (u_y=0)\)
Step 1: \(\text{ball 1: }y_1=h-\tfrac12gt^2,\quad x_1=u_xt\)
Step 2: \(\text{ball 2: }y_2=h-\tfrac12gt^2,\quad x_2=0\)
Worked derivation: \[y_1(t)=y_2(t)=0\Rightarrow t_1=t_2=\sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}\]
Check: \[h=5\ \mathrm m,\ g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}:\ t=\sqrt{\frac{10}{10}}=1\ \mathrm s\ \text{for both}\]
Why: \(a_x=0,\quad a_y=-g\ \ (\text{independent of }u_x)\)
Why not the others: (B) \(t_1=\sqrt{2h/g}\not<t_2\); (C) \(t_2=\sqrt{2h/g}\not<t_1\); (D) \(t=\sqrt{2h/g}\ \text{has no }u_x\).
Key point: \(t_{\text{fall}}=\sqrt{2h/g}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Power as a dot product and the rate of change of speed
questions.question: At an instant, a particle of mass 2 kg has velocity v=(3î+4ĵ) m/s, and the net force on it is F=(2î−ĵ) N. At what rate is its speed changing at this instant?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.2 m/s².
Given: \(m=2\ \mathrm{kg},\quad\mathbf v=(3\hat{\mathbf i}+4\hat{\mathbf j})\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\quad\mathbf F=(2\hat{\mathbf i}-\hat{\mathbf j})\ \mathrm N\)
Formula/Principle: \(P=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\tfrac12mv^2\right)=mv\dfrac{dv}{dt}\)
Step 1: \(P=(2)(3)+(-1)(4)=2\ \mathrm W\)
Step 2: \(v=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{dv}{dt}=\dfrac{P}{mv}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{2}{2\times5}=0.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\]
Check: \[a_t=\frac{\mathbf F\cdot\hat{\mathbf v}}{m}=\frac{(2)(0.6)+(-1)(0.8)}{2}=\frac{0.4}{2}=0.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\]
Why: \(\dfrac{dv}{dt}=a_t=\dfrac{\mathbf F\cdot\hat{\mathbf v}}{m}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{P}{m}=1.0\) (\(\div v\) omitted); (B) \(\dfrac{P}{v}=0.4\ \mathrm N\) (\(\div m\) omitted); (C) \(P=+2\ \mathrm W>0\Rightarrow\dfrac{dv}{dt}>0\).
Key point: \(\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=mv\,\dfrac{dv}{dt}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.question: The figure shows a uniform disc of original mass M and radius R with a circular hole of radius R/2 removed; its centre is R/2 from original centre O. About the perpendicular axis through O, what is the remaining moment of inertia?
questions.image_alt: An original disc centred at O has radius R; a circular hole of radius R/2 is centred at H, with OH=R/2, tangent to the original rim.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 13MR²/32.
Given: \(\text{disc }M,\ R;\quad\text{hole radius }\dfrac R2,\quad OH=\dfrac R2\)
Formula/Principle: \(I_{\text{remain}}=I_{\text{disc}}-I_{\text{hole},O};\quad I_O=I_{cm}+md^2\)
Step 1: \(m_{\text{hole}}=M\,\dfrac{\pi(R/2)^2}{\pi R^2}=\dfrac M4\)
Step 2: \(I_{\text{disc}}=\tfrac12MR^2\)
Step 3: \(I_{\text{hole},cm}=\tfrac12\cdot\dfrac M4\cdot\left(\dfrac R2\right)^2=\dfrac{MR^2}{32}\)
Step 4: \(m_{\text{hole}}d^2=\dfrac M4\cdot\left(\dfrac R2\right)^2=\dfrac{MR^2}{16}\)
Step 5: \(I_{\text{hole},O}=\dfrac{MR^2}{32}+\dfrac{2MR^2}{32}=\dfrac{3MR^2}{32}\)
Worked derivation: \[I_{\text{remain}}=\frac{16MR^2}{32}-\frac{3MR^2}{32}=\frac{13MR^2}{32}\]
Check: \[\frac{13}{32}MR^2<\frac12MR^2;\qquad m_{\text{remain}}=\frac34M\]
Why: \(I=\displaystyle\int r^2\,dm\ \text{additive}\Rightarrow I_{\text{remain}}=I_{\text{full}}-I_{\text{removed}}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac34MR^2=\tfrac38MR^2\) (remaining mass as a full disc); (B) \(\tfrac12-\tfrac1{32}=\tfrac{15}{32}\) (\(md^2\) omitted); (D) \(\tfrac12-\tfrac1{16}=\tfrac7{16}\) (\(I_{\text{hole},cm}\) omitted).
Key point: \(I_O=I_{cm}+md^2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Free-surface slope in an accelerating tank
questions.question: An open water tank accelerates to the right at g/2. In its frame, what is the magnitude of the steady free-surface slope, vertical rise divided by horizontal distance?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1/2.
Given: \(a=\dfrac g2\ (\text{to the right})\)
Formula/Principle: \(\mathbf g_{\text{eff}}=\mathbf g-\mathbf a;\quad\text{free surface}\perp\mathbf g_{\text{eff}};\quad\tan\theta=\dfrac ag\)
Step 1: \(\mathbf g_{\text{eff}}=-\dfrac g2\,\hat{\mathbf x}-g\,\hat{\mathbf y}\)
Step 2: \(\left|\dfrac{dh}{dx}\right|=\dfrac{a}{g}\)
Worked derivation: \[\left|\frac{dh}{dx}\right|=\frac{g/2}{g}=\frac12\]
Check: \[\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}=-\rho a,\ \frac{\partial p}{\partial y}=-\rho g:\quad dp=0\Rightarrow\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac ag=-\frac12\]
Why: \(dp=-\rho a\,dx-\rho g\,dy=0\ \text{on the free surface}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac ga=2\) (inverted); (C) \(1\) (\(a=g\)); (D) \(\dfrac14=\left(\dfrac ag\right)^2\).
Key point: \(\tan\theta=\dfrac ag\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two identical bodies of constant heat capacity C start at absolute temperatures T and 3T. Isolated together, they equilibrate without work. What is their total entropy change?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) C ln(4/3).
Given: \(C_1=C_2=C,\quad T_1=T,\quad T_2=3T,\quad W=0,\ Q_{\text{ext}}=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(C(T_f-T_1)+C(T_f-T_2)=0;\quad\Delta S=\displaystyle\int\frac{C\,dT}{T}=C\ln\frac{T_f}{T_i}\)
Step 1: \(2T_f=T+3T\Rightarrow T_f=2T\)
Step 2: \(\Delta S_1=C\ln\dfrac{2T}{T}=C\ln2\)
Step 3: \(\Delta S_2=C\ln\dfrac{2T}{3T}=C\ln\dfrac23\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta S=C\ln2+C\ln\frac23=C\ln\frac43\]
Check: \[\ln\frac43\approx0.288>0\]
Why: \(\text{isolated, irreversible}\Rightarrow\Delta S_{\text{total}}>0\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\Delta S=0\ \text{only if reversible}\); (C) \(C\ln\tfrac34<0\); (D) \(2C\ln2\) (\(\ln\tfrac23\) replaced by \(\ln2\)).
Key point: \(\Delta S=C\ln\dfrac{T_f^2}{T_1T_2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Phase difference from wave speed, frequency and separation
questions.question: A sinusoidal wave travels along a string at 12 m/s with frequency 4 Hz. At a fixed instant, what is the phase difference between two points of the string that are 0.5 m apart along the direction of propagation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) π/3.
Given: \(v=12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\quad f=4\ \mathrm{Hz},\quad\Delta x=0.5\ \mathrm m\)
Formula/Principle: \(\lambda=\dfrac vf,\quad\Delta\phi=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x\)
Step 1: \(\lambda=\dfrac{12}{4}=3\ \mathrm m\)
Step 2: \(\Delta\phi=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\times0.5\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta\phi=\frac{2\pi\times0.5}{3}=\frac{\pi}{3}\]
Check: \[\frac{\Delta x}{\lambda}=\frac{0.5}{3}=\frac16\Rightarrow\Delta\phi=\frac16\times2\pi=\frac\pi3\]
Why: \(\phi=kx-\omega t,\quad k=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{\pi\,\Delta x}{\lambda}=\dfrac\pi6\) (\(2\pi\to\pi\)); (B) \(\dfrac\pi2\Rightarrow\Delta x=\dfrac\lambda4=0.75\ \mathrm m\); (C) \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\Rightarrow\Delta x=\dfrac\lambda3=1.0\ \mathrm m\).
Key point: \(\Delta\phi=2\pi\dfrac{\Delta x}{\lambda}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Total energy of a circular satellite orbit
questions.question: A satellite of mass m orbits a planet of mass M in a circle of radius r. Taking potential energy zero at infinity, what is its total mechanical energy?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) −GMm/(2r).
Given: \(m,\ M,\ r;\quad U(\infty)=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{mv^2}{r}=\dfrac{GMm}{r^2},\quad U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r},\quad E=K+U\)
Step 1: \(mv^2=\dfrac{GMm}{r}\Rightarrow K=\tfrac12mv^2=\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\)
Step 2: \(U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}\)
Worked derivation: \[E=\frac{GMm}{2r}-\frac{GMm}{r}=-\frac{GMm}{2r}\]
Check: \[E=-K=\frac U2<0\ \ (\text{bound orbit})\]
Why: \(\text{gravity supplies the centripetal force}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(+\dfrac{GMm}{2r}=K\); (B) \(-\dfrac{GMm}{r}=U\); (D) \(E=0\Rightarrow\text{escape},\ v=\sqrt{2GM/r}\).
Key point: \(E=-K=\dfrac U2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Zero potential on a signed line
questions.question: The figure places +q at x=0 and −4q at x=3a, with a>0. At which finite points on the x-axis is the electric potential zero?
questions.image_alt: On a signed horizontal axis, +q is at x=0 and −4q is at x=3a, with the separation labelled 3a and a>0.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) x=−a and x=3a/5.
Given: \(+q\ \text{at }x=0,\quad-4q\ \text{at }x=3a\)
Formula/Principle: \(V=\dfrac{kq}{|x|}-\dfrac{4kq}{|x-3a|}\)
Step 1: \(V=0\Rightarrow|x-3a|=4|x|\)
Step 2: \(x<0:\ 3a-x=-4x\Rightarrow x=-a\)
Step 3: \(0<x<3a:\ 3a-x=4x\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{3a}{5}\)
Step 4: \(x>3a:\ x-3a=4x\Rightarrow x=-a\ (\text{not in }x>3a)\)
Worked derivation: \[x=-a,\qquad x=\frac{3a}{5}\]
Check: \[x=-a:\ \frac{kq}{a}-\frac{4kq}{4a}=0;\qquad x=\frac{3a}{5}:\ \frac{5kq}{3a}-\frac{4kq}{12a/5}=\frac{5kq}{3a}-\frac{5kq}{3a}=0\]
Why: \(V=0\iff\dfrac{r_2}{r_1}=4\)
Why not the others: (A) \(x=a:\ \dfrac{kq}{a}-\dfrac{4kq}{2a}=-\dfrac{kq}{a}\ne0\); (C) \(x=0,\ 3a:\ |V|\to\infty\); (D) \(x=-\dfrac{3a}{5}:\ \dfrac{5kq}{3a}-\dfrac{4kq}{18a/5}=\dfrac{5kq}{9a}\ne0\).
Key point: \(|q_1|/r_1=|q_2|/r_2\ \ (\text{opposite signs})\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Plate separation change at fixed battery voltage
questions.question: A parallel-plate capacitor stays connected to an ideal constant-voltage battery while plate separation is doubled, with area and dielectric unchanged. How do stored charge and energy change?
options: C) Charge halves but energy doubles
D) Charge stays fixed and energy halves
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both become half.
Given: \(V=\text{const},\quad d\to2d,\quad A,\ \varepsilon\ \text{unchanged}\)
Formula/Principle: \(C=\dfrac{\varepsilon A}{d},\quad Q=CV,\quad U=\tfrac12CV^2\)
Step 1: \(C_f=\dfrac{\varepsilon A}{2d}=\dfrac{C_i}{2}\)
Step 2: \(Q_f=C_fV=\dfrac{Q_i}{2}\)
Worked derivation: \[U_f=\frac12C_fV^2=\frac12\cdot\frac{C_i}{2}V^2=\frac{U_i}{2}\]
Check: \[W_{\text{battery}}=V(Q_f-Q_i)=-\tfrac12C_iV^2=-U_i;\quad W_{\text{agent}}=\Delta U-W_{\text{battery}}=-\tfrac12U_i+U_i=+\tfrac12U_i>0\]
Why: \(\text{battery connected}\Rightarrow V\ \text{fixed},\ Q\ \text{free to change}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(C_f=2C_i\) (\(C\propto d\)); (C) \(U=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}\ \text{with }Q\ \text{fixed}\); (D) \(Q\ \text{fixed}\ \text{only if disconnected}\).
Key point: \(V\ \text{fixed}:\ Q\propto C,\ U\propto C\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A cell of emf 12 V and internal resistance 2 Ω supplies a 4 Ω external resistor. What is the terminal voltage while it delivers current?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 8 V.
Given: \(\mathcal E=12\ \mathrm V,\quad r=2\ \Omega,\quad R=4\ \Omega\)
Formula/Principle: \(I=\dfrac{\mathcal E}{R+r},\quad V=\mathcal E-Ir=IR\)
Step 1: \(I=\dfrac{12}{4+2}=2\ \mathrm A\)
Worked derivation: \[V=\mathcal E-Ir=12-2\times2=8\ \mathrm V\]
Check: \[IR=2\times4=8\ \mathrm V\]
Why: \(\mathcal E=I(R+r)\)
Why not the others: (A) \(12\ \mathrm V=\mathcal E\) (\(Ir\) omitted); (B) \(Ir=4\ \mathrm V\) (drop inside the cell); (C) \(\dfrac{\mathcal E}{2}=6\ \mathrm V\) (\(R=r\)).
Key point: \(V=\mathcal E\,\dfrac{R}{R+r}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The plane of a single-turn loop of area A carrying current I makes 30° with a uniform magnetic field B. What is the torque magnitude?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (√3/2)IAB.
Given: \(\text{plane of loop at }30^\circ\ \text{to }\mathbf B;\quad N=1\)
Formula/Principle: \(\boldsymbol\tau=\boldsymbol\mu\times\mathbf B,\quad\mu=IA,\quad\tau=IAB\sin\theta\ \ (\theta=\angle(\hat{\mathbf n},\mathbf B))\)
Step 1: \(\theta=90^\circ-30^\circ=60^\circ\)
Worked derivation: \[\tau=IAB\sin60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}IAB\]
Check: \[\tau=IAB\cos30^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}IAB\]
Why: \(\hat{\mathbf n}\perp\text{plane of loop}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(IAB\sin30^\circ=\tfrac12IAB\) (plane angle used as \(\theta\)); (B) \(IAB\) (\(\theta=90^\circ\)); (D) \(\theta=0^\circ\).
Key point: \(\tau=NIAB\sin\theta,\ \theta\ \text{from the normal}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: An ideal transformer has 200 primary turns and 50 secondary turns. Its primary is at 240 V rms; the secondary drives a 6 Ω resistive load. What are secondary voltage and primary current?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 60 V and 2.5 A.
Given: \(N_p=200,\quad N_s=50,\quad V_p=240\ \mathrm V,\quad R=6\ \Omega\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{N_s}{N_p},\quad I_s=\dfrac{V_s}{R},\quad V_pI_p=V_sI_s\)
Step 1: \(V_s=240\times\dfrac{50}{200}=60\ \mathrm V\)
Step 2: \(I_s=\dfrac{60}{6}=10\ \mathrm A\)
Step 3: \(P=V_sI_s=600\ \mathrm W\)
Worked derivation: \[I_p=\frac{600}{240}=2.5\ \mathrm A\]
Check: \[\frac{I_p}{I_s}=\frac{N_s}{N_p}=\frac14\Rightarrow I_p=\frac{10}{4}=2.5\ \mathrm A\]
Why: \(\text{ideal}\Rightarrow P_{\text{in}}=P_{\text{out}}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(I_s=10\ \mathrm A\ne I_p\); (C) \(V_s=V_p=240\ \mathrm V\) (turns ratio ignored); (D) \(V_s=\dfrac{240}{2}=120\ \mathrm V\) (\(N_s/N_p=\tfrac12\)).
Key point: \(\dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{I_p}{I_s}=\dfrac{N_s}{N_p}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Optical path and the extra phase introduced by a slab
questions.question: Light of vacuum wavelength 600 nm crosses a transparent slab of thickness 3.0 μm normally. The slab has refractive index 1.5. Compared with the same 3.0 μm of vacuum, what extra phase does the slab introduce?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 5π.
Given: \(\lambda=600\ \mathrm{nm},\quad L=3.0\ \mu\mathrm m=3000\ \mathrm{nm},\quad n=1.5\)
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta=(n-1)L,\quad\Delta\phi=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta\)
Step 1: \(\Delta=(1.5-1)(3000\ \mathrm{nm})=1500\ \mathrm{nm}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{\Delta}{\lambda}=\dfrac{1500}{600}=2.5\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta\phi=2\pi\times2.5=5\pi\]
Check: \[\phi_{\text{slab}}=\frac{2\pi(1.5)(3000)}{600}=15\pi,\quad\phi_{\text{vac}}=\frac{2\pi(3000)}{600}=10\pi,\quad15\pi-10\pi=5\pi\]
Why: \(\lambda_{\text{slab}}=\dfrac{\lambda}{n}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(15\pi=\phi_{\text{slab}}\) (vacuum phase not subtracted); (C) \(10\pi=\phi_{\text{vac}}\); (D) \(\pi\times2.5\) (\(2\pi\to\pi\)).
Key point: \(\Delta\phi=\dfrac{2\pi(n-1)L}{\lambda}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Propagation from E and B orientation
questions.question: An electromagnetic plane wave has electric field along +y and magnetic field along +z. What direction does it propagate?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) +x.
Given: \(\mathbf E\parallel+\hat{\mathbf y},\quad\mathbf B\parallel+\hat{\mathbf z}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\hat{\mathbf k}_{\text{prop}}\parallel\mathbf E\times\mathbf B\)
Step 1: \(\hat{\mathbf y}\times\hat{\mathbf z}=\hat{\mathbf x}\)
Worked derivation: \[\mathbf S=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B\parallel\hat{\mathbf y}\times\hat{\mathbf z}=+\hat{\mathbf x}\]
Check: \[\hat{\mathbf x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf y}=0,\qquad\hat{\mathbf x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}=0\]
Why: \(\mathbf E\perp\mathbf B\perp\hat{\mathbf k}_{\text{prop}}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\mathbf y}=-\hat{\mathbf x}\) (order reversed); (B) \(+\hat{\mathbf y}\parallel\mathbf E\); (C) \(+\hat{\mathbf z}\parallel\mathbf B\).
Key point: \(\mathbf S=\dfrac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Two half-lives: activity and surviving fraction
questions.question: Equal initial numbers N₀ of nuclides X and Y have half-lives 2 h and 4 h. After 8 h, find (i) activity ratio AX:AY and (ii) fraction of all initial nuclei still undecayed.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1:2 and 5/32.
Given: \(N_{0X}=N_{0Y}=N_0,\quad T_X=2\ \mathrm h,\quad T_Y=4\ \mathrm h,\quad t=8\ \mathrm h\)
Formula/Principle: \(N=N_0\,2^{-t/T},\quad A=\lambda N,\quad\lambda=\dfrac{\ln2}{T}\)
Step 1: \(N_X=N_0\,2^{-8/2}=\dfrac{N_0}{16}\)
Step 2: \(N_Y=N_0\,2^{-8/4}=\dfrac{N_0}{4}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{\lambda_X}{\lambda_Y}=\dfrac{T_Y}{T_X}=2\)
Step 4: \(\dfrac{A_X}{A_Y}=\dfrac{\lambda_XN_X}{\lambda_YN_Y}=2\times\dfrac{1/16}{1/4}=\dfrac12\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{N_X+N_Y}{2N_0}=\frac{\tfrac1{16}+\tfrac14}{2}=\frac{5/16}{2}=\frac{5}{32}\]
Check: \[\text{decayed fraction}=1-\frac{5}{32}=\frac{27}{32}\]
Why: \(A=-\dfrac{dN}{dt}=\lambda N\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{N_X}{N_Y}=\dfrac14\) (\(\lambda\) ratio omitted); (B) \(\dfrac{\lambda_X}{\lambda_Y}=2\) (\(N\) ratio omitted); (D) \(\dfrac{27}{32}=\text{decayed fraction}\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{A_X}{A_Y}=\dfrac{T_Y}{T_X}\cdot\dfrac{N_X}{N_Y}\)
